full_instruction: Write a historical fiction story about a volunteer nurse working in an overcrowded field hospital during the 1918 influenza pandemic. She keeps a private tally of patient names in the margins of a hymn book, unable to bear a formal ledger of the dead. Set the story during a single thirty-six-hour shift when the hospital runs out of gauze. Write the entire story in present tense to convey the immediacy of the crisis. During the story, reveal that the nurse has been quietly hiding her own influenza symptoms so she can keep working. End with the nurse finally collapsing at her post just as a relief shift arrives.

constraints.requirement: Protagonist is a volunteer nurse working in an overcrowded field hospital during the 1918 influenza pandemic
She keeps a private tally of patient names in the margins of a hymn book, unable to bear a formal ledger of the dead
Set the story during a single thirty-six-hour shift when the hospital runs out of gauze
Write the entire story in present tense to convey the immediacy of the crisis
Reveal that the nurse has been quietly hiding her own influenza symptoms so she can keep working
End with the nurse finally collapsing at her post just as a relief shift arrives

text:
The canvas walls of the tent do not hold the winter wind out; they hold the fever in.

Elara Vance tightens her apron, but her hands tremble slightly beneath the fabric stiff with sweat and the ghostly residue of days' worth of snot, soot, and despair. Outside the main triage flap, the mud of Camp Liberty churns into a slick, brown slurry by boots that never stop walking. Inside, however, it is hotter than the sun outside could ever be. The air shimmers with a palpable weight, thick with the smell of antiseptic vinegar trying desperately to mask the underlying rot of wet wool and dying lungs.

"Another one," calls out Miller, the orderlies' foreman, his voice cracking like dry timber. He shoves a stretcher through the gap between the cots, where hundreds lie packed shoulder-to-shoulder like sardines in a tin can. "From Quarantine Row. She's blue all over."

Elara does not flinch. Not anymore. To flinch is to invite the virus inside; it is to break the rhythm that keeps her from collapsing herself. Yet, as she grabs the basin and steps onto the narrow gangway strung between the bunks, a sharp pain spikes behind her eyes. She knows what that headache feels like: it is the signature of the Spanish Flu, the very thing killing them all around her.

She forces the grimace down. She cannot stop. If she stops, Miller will ask if she is fit for duty. If she says she is sick, they will send her home to a bed in a quiet house, leaving this hell to someone else who might not be as strong as she pretends to be.

"Miss Vance," a voice whispers from beneath a pile of blankets. It is Private Thomas. His skin has taken on the color of old parchment, waxy and translucent. "The cough... it sounds like stones grinding."

Elara kneels beside him, placing a cool hand on his forehead. Her own palm burns with her fever, but she ignores it to check the heat radiating from his. It is too high. "I know, Tommy," she says softly, forcing her voice to remain steady despite the dryness in her throat and the way her chest feels heavy, as if filled with wet sand. She remembers last night when she tried to sleep; her nose was running so thickly it woke the entire ward. She had used a washcloth to clear it, then pressed hard against her temples until the throbbing stopped enough to let her stand. Now, standing here among the dying, she feels the familiar chill rising in her limbs, but she hides it behind a mask of professional calm. "Just breathe with me. In... and out."

She works with mechanical precision, though her steps are slightly unsteady. She checks the temperature of the next patient, then the one after. She hands out small cups of water to those who can swallow, ignoring the ones who have lost the ability entirely. The influenza is not a respecter of rank or age; it hunts the weak, the exhausted, and the young alike. It is a silent killer that turns bright eyes hollow in an hour.

By midday, the hospital groans. The canvas roof sags under the collective weight of a thousand ragged breaths. Elara moves between the rows, her eyes scanning for the tell-tale signs: the cyanosis of lips, the glassy stare, the sudden, terrifying stillness before the final gasp. She feels dizzy now, the room tilting slightly as she leans over a cot. She grips the side of the bedframe hard to steady herself, hiding the tremor in her legs from the other nurses passing by. She is burning up, her skin hot to the touch even through her uniform, but she knows that if anyone notices her temperature, they will pull her from this tent before the end of her shift.

It is then she stops. Her fingers brush the pocket where she keeps her supply kit, and her stomach drops with a lurch that has nothing to do with the fever. Empty. The box of gauze, usually her most precious commodity, is gone. The last roll has been used on a wound that has already cauterized itself, but there are no more bandages for the bleeding noses, the weeping eyes, or the lungs that need to be kept clear of mucus and blood.

"Miller!" she shouts, her voice cutting through the din, though it sounds hoarse and strained to her own ears. "Where are the dressings?"

"I don't know, Elara!" Miller yells back from the supply tent entrance. "The wagon left hours ago! The requisition officer said we're down to the last batch, and it's all gone!"

Elara stares at him. There is no way to ask for more. The trains are stalled; the roads are impassable; the influenza has overwhelmed the logistical chain before anyone could react. They are running blind, with nothing to stop the hemorrhage. And she is running on borrowed time herself, her own immune system crumbling while she fights to keep others upright.

She finds Corporal Halloway sitting upright against the wall, staring into the gloom of the tent's entrance. He is holding a photograph—a black-and-white print of his daughter in a garden he will never see again.

"Water," Elara says gently, offering the cup she has filled from her canteen, though her own mouth feels parched with thirst.

Halloway does not look at her. "Does it end?" he asks, his voice a dry rasp.

"No," Elara replies, knowing this is a question without an answer. She leans closer, ignoring the sharp pain shooting through her jaw as she exhales—a symptom she has been suppressing since dawn. "But we are still here."

He takes the cup with shaking hands and drinks, spilling some on the straw mattress. He closes his eyes, and within moments, the rhythmic breathing that has been his lifeline for twenty years slows to a halt. The silence that follows is not peaceful; it is heavy, suffocating, and filled with the sound of other lungs struggling in the rows behind him.

Elara stays kneeling for a long time. She watches her hands, stained permanently now with dark stains from soot and blood, unable to be scrubbed clean no matter how many times she washes them. The official ledger is already full; the clerks at headquarters have stacked pages of paper high in their offices, recording names with cold, bureaucratic efficiency that makes Elara's skin crawl. It reduces souls to ink blots, strips away the stories, the fears, and the hopes that live inside those chests. She cannot bear to add another name to that sterile list without knowing how he has died.

Instead, she reaches into her coat pocket and pulls out a small, tattered hymn book belonging to a chaplain who has been evacuated weeks ago. The pages are yellowed and dog-eared, smelling faintly of old lavender and church wax.

On the bottom margin of Psalm 23, in a cramped, hurried scrawl, she writes: *Corporal Halloway.*

She turns the page to *Amazing Grace*. There, she adds his age: *Age 34.* And a small note: *Held his daughter's photo tightly until he stopped breathing. Died with no gauze on his chest.*

On the next page, near the verse about valleys of shadow and death, she writes the name of Private Thomas: *Thomas Gentry. Age 19. Last words: "Tell my sister I saw the birds."* She adds a small mark beside it: *No bandage for bleeding nose.*

The tent is chaotic around her—cries from the fevered, the shuffling of orderlies, the clatter of basins—but in the margin of that hymn book, there is a quiet intimacy. As she turns to the next page, ready to record the fate of the boy shivering in the corner, she pauses. Her vision swims; her head thumps against her own will. The ink feels heavy in her pen, not from fatigue, but from the sheer weight of the lives being extinguished without even the basic dignity of a clean cloth on their skin. And beneath it all, her own body betrays her. Her nose is running freely now, dripping onto her sleeve, a clear sign that she, too, is one of the infected, fighting to stay in the line of fire.

She wipes her nose quickly with the back of her hand, hiding the evidence from everyone except herself. She dips the pen again. The world outside might think of them as statistics, casualties to be tallied in a report for the war's end. But here, under the canvas roof, Elara keeps their names safe, preserving their humanity against the eroding force of the pandemic and her own lack of supplies. She is not just a nurse; she is the keeper of their memories, writing a private epitaph in the margins of faith before the silence takes them all. Even as her own lungs begin to tighten and her knees buckle, she anchors herself with willpower alone.

A young soldier, barely sixteen, lies shivering in the corner, his breath hitching in a high-pitched whine. Elara scoots over, ignoring the proximity to the dying. She wraps her scarf around his neck and begins to hum a tune she remembers from before the war, a simple folk song about harvest moons and safe returns. Her voice wavers at first, then steadies as she fights back the cough that wants to tear its way out of her throat.

The boy's eyes flutter open. "Who are you?" he whispers, confusion clouding his mind.

"I'm Elara," she says, leaning in close so her voice carries over the din of the tent, forcing a smile that doesn't reach her feverish eyes. "And I'm not going anywhere."

She opens the hymn book to a fresh page and waits for the next name to be written, her pen ready, her heart heavy with the knowledge that every line added is a life permanently lost, yet never forgotten by those who love them. Around them, the rhythm of life and death continues its relentless dance, but in the quiet margins of her book, they remain distinct, real, and remembered, even if she cannot bandage their wounds anymore, and even as her own strength fades with every passing hour.

The hours blur together into a gray, fevered haze. The sun dips below the horizon, casting long shadows across the rows of cots, but the noise inside never stops. Elara's vision blurs further. The margin of the book swims in front of her eyes. Her pen slips from her fingers, rolling off the edge of the page and disappearing into the dark space beneath the cot.

She tries to lift it again, but the weight is too great. Her chest heaves, a violent cough rattling her frame, bringing fresh waves of pain that make her gasp. She leans forward, trying to steady herself against the side of the cot, but the world tilts violently. The canvas walls seem to warp and breathe around her.

"Miller!" she croaks out, the sound barely rising above a wheeze. "Miller..."

No answer comes immediately. The din of the dying seems to swell, drowning out her call. Her legs give way completely. She slumps forward, the hymn book slipping from her lap to the straw mattress below, opening to a page that now floats in front of her face like a ghostly map.

"Miss Vance? Miss Vance!" Miller's voice cuts through the haze, louder and more urgent now. "We're here! The new shift is here!"

Footsteps thunder down the gangway, heavy and numerous. Hands reach out to steady her, but Elara is already sliding down, her body giving up the fight she has been fighting for thirty-six hours. She closes her eyes as her vision goes black, the last thing she sees before darkness takes her is the open book resting on the floor, the margins filled with names of strangers who will never know they were remembered.

She is still in the hospital. She is still at her post. But the nurse has finally collapsed, a silent sentinel falling amidst the endless tide of influenza, leaving the hymn book and its fragile tally as the only witness to her sacrifice.
